title: Clay, drop, clot, bone, flesh
hookLine: the stages of a human's making, then another creation (23:12–14)
last: KHUSHU' — NOT MORE WORDS, SLOWER BODIES.

cards: Put two fingers on the inside of your wrist. Wait a second. There.
That small, steady knock has been going since before you were born, and you didn't start it. Nobody asked whether you wanted a heartbeat, or bones, or the particular shape of your hands.
Al-Mu'minun, just after describing the believers, tells how any human being is made, from the very beginning. It takes three verses, and it ends with a sentence of pure praise.

teach.h: AN EXTRACT OF CLAY, THEN A DROP.
teach.b: The verses move in steps, and each step has a word. First, a sulala min tin, an extract of clay, an essence drawn from the earth. Then a nutfa, a drop, placed in a safe lodging.
Then the drop becomes an 'alaqa, a word Pickthall translates clot; its root carries the sense of something that clings. Then a mudgha, a little lump; the word means something chewed.
Then bones, and the bones are clothed with flesh.
Clay, drop, clot, bone, flesh. Then the turn.
Pickthall: "and then produced it as another creation. So blessed be Allah, the Best of creators!" Another creation. After all the stages comes something that isn't just one more stage.
Some commentators, citing reports from Ibn 'Abbas, read this as the moment the spirit is breathed in: the lump of tissue becomes someone.
Some modern writers have compared these verses to modern embryology, and others caution against reading them as a science textbook. Either way, the verse doesn't end in a lab report.

It ends in tabarak, blessed. Commentators tell a story that a companion, hearing these verses for the first time, said the closing praise aloud before it was recited, and was told that's exactly how it ends.
It's a story people tell, and its chain is debated. But it shows how the passage feels: you climb the stages, and the praise is the natural top of the stairs.

how: Many Muslims recite 23:12–14 when reflecting on human creation, and the closing phrase 'fa tabarak Allahu ahsanu l-khaliqin' is said by some on seeing a newborn or something beautifully made.

practice: Put two fingers on your wrist or the side of your neck, count a few beats, then stop counting and just feel them.

Think of the stages it took to get here: earth, a drop, a lump, bones, flesh, and then whatever it is that makes you you. If you pray, you can say the verse's ending: blessed is God, the best of creators.

wordCard.voice: Clay. Where the human story starts in this surah: an extract of clay, then drop, clot, lump, bone and flesh, then another creation. Today's word.
